item.title: The limits of magic-state cultivation
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Harmless faults in postselected non-Clifford circuits are determined by stabilizer projection on an underlying code defined on the t non-Clifford gates. Cultivation checks using GHZ folds halve fault tolerance to d=(δ+1)/2 on distance-δ codes, whereas verified cat checks preserve full distance d=δ, certified up to δ=9.

Grade 0.500 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Llorencc Balada Gaggioli, Jakub Marevcek

Figure

Real-T fault distance compared to target code distance δ. Unverified GHZ folds achieve only d=(δ+1)/2, while verified cat architectures preserve full distance d=δ up to δ=9.

Asks

Which faults are harmful in magic-state cultivation circuits containing real non-Clifford gates, and how can cultivation checks maintain the full code distance?

Before

Clifford S-proxy designs predicted fault distance equal to code distance δ, but real-T simulations showed distance drops to (δ+1)/2 for δ=3,5.

But

Deterministic postselected single-qubit target states (|T⟩ or |CCZ⟩) with no stabilizing Pauli operators besides identity; ideal noiseless final stabilizer decoding stage unless explicit noisy schedule is modeled.

Tools

Clifford skeleton decomposition · stabilizer code projection · verified cat checks · exhaustive fault path search

Abstract

Fault tolerance is understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits such as magic-state cultivation, which checks an encoded T state with physical T gates, have therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful. We develop such a theory and show that, for any circuit that prepares a magic state with non-Clifford gates and postselection, one stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful. This ties cultivation to distillation, bounds its T-count from below and gives an exact test. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the code. As a use case, we analyze the S gates that have stood in for T gates in the design of cultivation. We show that this proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and that the checks in use, on color and surface codes, tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that keep the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.

item.title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Formalized reaction depth. Proved any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be executed with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth using homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs) plus Toffoli states, at exponential space cost leaving dirty qubits.

Grade 0.496 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Christopher Kang, Alexander Cowtan, Adam Bene Watts, Guillaume Dauphinais, Benjamin Ide

Asks

How can reaction depth be formalized, and how efficiently can coherent Boolean logic be implemented in fault-tolerant quantum architectures using restricted PPM operations?

But

Requires exponential space overhead and leaves ancillary qubits dirty; uncomputation in practical adder and multiplier designs requires heterogeneous PPMs.

Tools

Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs) · LDPC code gateset · Toffoli state injection · AutoAND circuits

Abstract

Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program. In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection. We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

item.title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Universal fault-tolerant quantum computation requires only a constant number (le20) of external control wires on an n-qubit chip, executing n/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀(n/ϵ) logical qubits with depth-3 periodic geometrically local operations.

Grade 0.494 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Christopher A. Pattison, Jeongwan Haah, John Preskill

Figure

Unrolling of a 1D brickwork quantum circuit into a 2D tile where qubits propagate continuously upward across a physical planar lattice.

Asks

How much external control is strictly necessary to operate a fault-tolerant universal quantum processor?

But

Asymptotic analysis. Assumes a noiseless global clock and physical noise on all operations below a universal positive constant. Logical gate time is n/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀(n/ϵ) without instantaneous classical wires.

Tools

spacetime unrolling into 2D tiles · concatenated quantum codes · periodic depth-3 cellular automata · fault-tolerant instruction decoding

Abstract

Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with n physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~n/sfpolylog(n/ε) logical qubits, where ε is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~n/sfpolylog(n/ε); an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to sfpolylog(n/ε).

item.title: High-rate low-distance color codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Two-dimensional color codes reach optimal encoding rates of 1/3 at distance 3 and 1/4 at distance 4. In a linear ion chain model, simulated [[20,4,4]] and [[16,4,4]] codes hit break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of 0.22% and 0.26%.

Grade 0.482 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Peter-Jan H. S. Derks, Lucas Berent, Mark Webster, Robert Wille, Jens Eisert, Aleksander Kubica

Figure

Break-even two-qubit gate infidelity plotted against total qubits required per QEC cycle across distance-3 and distance-4 2D color codes. Shows [[16,4,4]] and [[20,4,4]] breaking even above 2×10−3 physical error rate using 36 to 46 qubits.

Asks

What are the optimal encoding rates for small, low-distance 2D color codes, and can they achieve break-even performance in trapped-ion chains?

Before

Bivariate bicycle codes with weight-5 stabilizers required [[30,4,5]] and [[48,4,7]] implementations with Shor-style extraction (Wang et al. 2024).

But

Numerical simulation only. Holds strictly for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with Euler characteristic χ≥0.

Tools

Steane-style error correction · Linear trapped-ion chain circuit-level noise model · Real-time feedback without post-selection · Tesseract / lookup-table decoding

Code. https://github.com/peter-janderks/small_color_codes

Abstract

Experimental implementations of two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have surpassed the fidelity of physical qubits. A natural next step is to investigate higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits. Here we propose small, high-rate 2D color codes for this purpose. We design distance-3 codes with encoding rates up to 1/3 and distance-4 codes with encoding rates up to 1/4. We prove that these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic. We benchmark the codes by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity. The two best-performing codes have parameters [[20,4,4]] and [[16,4,4]] and achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of 0.22% and 0.26%, respectively. These results match the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes that use weight-5 measurements.

item.title: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Using a stationary entangled singlet partner to flag bit flips on a shuttled ancilla restores circuit distance from 1-4 up to 5 or 6 on weight-8 and weight-10 codes, raising the Gross code [[144,12,12]] circuit distance from 7 to 10 in both bases.

Grade 0.482 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · William Chow, Jonathan Baugh

Figure

Logical error rate per round versus physical error rate p for distance-6 codes of weights 6, 8, and 10 decoded via BP+OSD and exact integer programming. Exact decoding reveals gains of up to 70x-90x over CAbLECAR that BP+OSD underreports.

Asks

Can preparing a mobile shuttling ancilla as part of an entangled spin singlet catch propagating hook errors and restore circuit distance in qLDPC syndrome extraction?

Before

CAbLECAR mobile ancillas kept only three-eighths to three-quarters of code distance, falling to circuit distance 1 at check weight 12.

But

Circuit-level Pauli noise model only, shuttling routing uses heuristic schedules, and exact distances are schedule-dependent.

Tools

singlet-flag syndrome extraction · circuit-level Pauli noise simulation · exact integer-program decoding via HiGHS · BP+OSD decoding

Abstract

High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from 3-7x to 5-17x for the weight-6 BB code, and from 1-12x to 5-90x at weights 8 and 10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.

item.title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — QuFrame closes the QEC feedback loop within a 1 µs round budget with fallback decoding in 144 ns, cutting the logical error rate by an average of 38.5% compared to a serialized blocking baseline.

Grade 0.469 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Aleksandra Świerkowska, Ilgaz Er, Emmanouil Giortamis, Pramod Bhatotia

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate scaling factor for a rotated surface code (d=3, 9 rounds). QuFrame avoids stalling and tracks closest to the ideal zero-latency baseline, outperforming the serialized blocking controller across all noise levels.

Asks

How can a quantum controller track the Pauli frame in real time with bounded per-instruction latency under multi-core dispatch and decoders of variable latency?

Before

A serialized blocking controller, as modeled in XQsim (Byun et al., 2022), increased logical error rates by up to 4.1× over an ideal zero-latency controller.

But

Evaluated on a distance-3 rotated surface code with 17 physical qubits; IBM Heron coherence times prolonged 10× in simulations; fallback lookup table memory scales poorly for higher code distances without truncation.

Tools

QuFrameISA · Instruction Resolution Engine (IRE) · Pauli Frame Management Unit (versioned compare-and-swap) · AMD Alveo V80 FPGA · Helios simulator with IBM Heron noise model

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict 1 μs cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within 1 μs while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. item.title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Generalizes pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution to state-dependent operations without approximation. Reaches up to 24× higher throughput than CUDA-Q on distance-3 topological memories with amplitude damping, and up to 83× higher throughput on 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements.

Grade 0.457 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Louis Follet, Paavai Pari, Isidor Schoch, Thien Nguyen, Justin G. Lietz, Daniel Lowell, Brucek Khailany, Krysta M. Svore, Dirk R. Englund, Taylor L. Patti

Figure

Throughput speedup of generalized PTSBE over CUDA-Q and Clifft as a function of non-Clifford gate fraction and total shots across surface codes, color codes, and 16-to-30-qubit random circuits.

Asks

Can pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution be extended to circuits with mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels without approximation?

Before

Original PTSBE required stochastic outcomes to be state-independent (mixtures of unitaries), excluding mid-circuit measurements and non-twirled amplitude damping.

But

Single-precision statevectors; limited by GPU memory for caching intermediate state branches (requires 8⋅2n bytes per cached state, e.g., 8 GiB per state at n=30 qubits).

Tools

generalized pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) · delayed inner product algorithm · GPU statevector simulator (CUDA-Q extension) · multinomial branching and cached state reuse

Abstract

Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.

item.title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Families of qubit CSS codes achieve X and Z distances DX,DZ≥cεN/(log⁡N)2 and 𝒦≥N1−ε encoded qubits per block, supporting 𝐬≥N1−ε disjoint matched triples of logical qubits with individually addressable logical CCZ gates selectable via a single transversal physical CCZ layer.

Grade 0.454 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Guanyu Zhu

Figure

Schematic workflow: expanding covers with complex character bounds provide code distance, finite field characters give common classical codewords for cocycles, and dual cycle functionals allow independent selection of transversal CCZ gates via balanced product complexes.

Asks

Can quantum LDPC codes achieve nearly linear code distance while supporting an almost linear number of individually addressable, transversal non-Clifford logical CCZ gates?

Before

was a single nontrivial transversal logical CCZ gate at distance N/polylog(N) (Li et al. 2024), or almost linear addressable CCZ yield with polynomial subsystem distance (Golowich et al. 2024)

But

Contingent on Assumption 1.1 (uniform subfield product expansion of Reed–Solomon codes). Requires initializing all logical qubits outside the 𝐬 selected triples to |0⟩.

Tools

balanced products of expanding graph covers · uniform subfield product expansion of Reed–Solomon codes · cup products of cellular sheaves on cubes · evaluation functionals on group algebras

Abstract

Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances Ω_ε(N/log²N) and at least N^(1-ε) individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed 0<ε<1. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to |0⟩, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent γ→0 and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares N^(1-ε) encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance Ω_ε(N/log²N). The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.
